title: Renovation Sentence Repair
description: Repair fragments, run-ons, and punctuation problems in a practical memo.
subject: rla
passage:
A neighborhood community center will close one meeting room for renovation next week. Staff members are editing a memo that explains the temporary room changes, the construction schedule, and the location of evening programs. Because the memo contains several dates and conditions, sentence boundaries must be especially clear.

The first draft includes a few fragments created when dependent clauses were separated from the sentences they belong to. It also contains run-ons in which two complete ideas were joined only with a comma. The editor checks each sentence for a subject and a complete verb, then decides whether related complete clauses should be separated with a period, joined with a semicolon, or connected with a comma and an appropriate coordinating conjunction.

Punctuation inside sentences also matters. Nonessential information may need commas so readers can see the core sentence. A colon can introduce a list after a complete clause, but it should not be inserted directly after a verb when the sentence flows naturally into the list. The memo should feel simple, yet the punctuation must show exactly where one thought ends and the next begins.

questions.explanation: The sentence has a subject, a complete verb, and a complete thought.
questions.rule: If a sentence starts with because/while/after, check whether a main clause completes it.

options.text: Because the east room will be closed for painting.
options.whyWrong: This is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone.

options.text: The east room will be closed for painting next Tuesday.
While crews replace the ceiling panels.
options.whyWrong: The clause begins with 'while' and lacks a main clause.

options.text: After the evening programs move upstairs.
options.whyWrong: This is an introductory dependent phrase, not a complete sentence.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct revision: “The room closes Tuesday, evening classes move upstairs.”
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
questions.rule: Two complete clauses need a period, semicolon, or comma plus a coordinating conjunction.

options.text: The room closes Tuesday, evening classes move upstairs.
options.whyWrong: A comma alone cannot join these two independent clauses.

options.text: The room closes Tuesday because. Evening classes move upstairs.
options.whyWrong: 'Because' is incomplete and creates a fragment.

options.text: The room closes Tuesday evening classes move upstairs.
options.whyWrong: Without punctuation or a connector, the sentence is fused.

options.text: The room closes Tuesday; evening classes move upstairs.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct punctuation: “The west room, which normally hosts art classes, {{blank}} remain open.”
questions.explanation: The nonessential clause is already enclosed by commas, and no punctuation belongs between the subject and 'will remain'.
questions.rule: Remove the nonessential clause mentally; the core sentence should still read smoothly.

options.text: will
, will
options.whyWrong: The opening comma already begins the nonessential clause; an extra comma before the verb would incorrectly separate subject and verb.

options.text: ; will
options.whyWrong: A semicolon cannot separate the subject from its verb.

options.text: : will
options.whyWrong: A colon cannot separate the subject from its verb.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct revision: “Staff will post signs at three locations the lobby, elevator, and west entrance.”
questions.explanation: The complete clause ends with 'locations,' and the colon correctly introduces the list.
questions.rule: Use a colon after a complete clause that announces what follows.

options.text: Staff will post signs at: three locations the lobby, elevator, and west entrance.
options.whyWrong: A colon should not interrupt the phrase 'at three locations'.

options.text: Staff will post signs: at three locations, the lobby, elevator, and west entrance.
options.whyWrong: The wording before the colon does not introduce the list cleanly.

options.text: Staff will post signs at three locations: the lobby, elevator, and west entrance.
Staff will post signs at three locations; the lobby, elevator, and west entrance.
options.whyWrong: A semicolon should not introduce a simple list fragment.

questions.prompt: Which revision fixes the comma splice? “The renovation starts Monday, it should finish by Friday.”
questions.explanation: A comma plus 'and' correctly joins the two independent clauses.
questions.rule: If both sides can stand alone, a comma needs a coordinating conjunction to join them.

options.text: The renovation starts Monday, it should finish by Friday.
options.whyWrong: The comma splice remains unchanged.

options.text: The renovation starts Monday because, it should finish by Friday.
options.whyWrong: The connector is incomplete and the comma is misplaced.

options.text: The renovation starts Monday it should finish by Friday.
options.whyWrong: Removing the comma creates a fused sentence.

options.text: The renovation starts Monday, and it should finish by Friday.

questions.explanation: The essential that-clause follows 'said' without punctuation.
questions.rule: Do not insert punctuation just because a sentence feels long; identify the clause relationship first.

options.text: The contractor said, that the hallway would stay open.
options.whyWrong: A comma should not separate 'said' from the essential that-clause.

options.text: The contractor said that the hallway would stay open.
The contractor said; that the hallway would stay open.
options.whyWrong: A semicolon cannot introduce a dependent that-clause.

options.text: The contractor said: that the hallway would stay open.
options.whyWrong: A colon is unnecessary before the that-clause.

questions.prompt: Choose the revision that fixes the sentence while preserving both the contrast and the cause: “Although the gym remains open, some programs will move outside, the east room is closed for painting.”
questions.explanation: The although-clause stays attached to the main clause, and the because-clause correctly explains why some programs will move outside.
questions.rule: With several clauses, check both grammar and meaning: each connector must attach to the idea it actually explains.

options.text: Although the gym remains open, some programs will move outside because the east room is closed for painting.
Although the gym remains open; some programs will move outside because the east room is closed for painting.
options.whyWrong: The semicolon incorrectly separates the dependent although-clause from the main clause.

options.text: Although the gym remains open, some programs will move outside; because the east room is closed for painting.
options.whyWrong: The semicolon leaves the because-clause as a dependent fragment instead of attaching it to the idea it explains.

options.text: Although the gym remains open because the east room is closed for painting, some programs will move outside.
options.whyWrong: This version is grammatical, but it changes the meaning by making the room closure explain why the gym remains open rather than why programs move outside.

questions.prompt: Which revision correctly keeps the information in one sentence while showing both the room identification and the contrast?
questions.explanation: The colon identifies the one available room, and the semicolon plus however correctly connects the contrasting independent clause about its limited capacity.
questions.rule: When one sentence has more than one boundary job, test each mark separately: what introduces, what joins, and what shows the relationship?

options.text: One room will remain available; the small conference room on the first floor, however, it seats only twelve people.
options.whyWrong: The semicolon is followed by a noun phrase rather than an independent clause, and the later comma does not correctly join the contrast.

options.text: One room will remain available: the small conference room on the first floor, however, it seats only twelve people.
options.whyWrong: The colon correctly introduces the room, but a comma alone cannot connect that completed identification to the independent clause introduced by however.

options.text: One room will remain available: the small conference room on the first floor; however, it seats only twelve people.
One room will remain available: the small conference room on the first floor; however: it seats only twelve people.
options.whyWrong: The semicolon can introduce the contrasting independent clause, but a colon does not belong after the conjunctive adverb however.
